paragraphs.heading: The mistaken belief
paragraphs.text: The gambler's fallacy, which also goes by the names Monte Carlo fallacy and fallacy of the maturity of chances, is a belief about independent outcomes that are equally likely. It says that an outcome which has turned up less often than expected is now more likely to come next, or the reverse. A dice player might think a 4 is due because few 4s have appeared lately. In fact every roll is independent, so the chance of a 4 stays 1/6 each time.

paragraphs.heading: Coins have no memory
paragraphs.text: Five heads in a row has a probability of 1/32, a little over 3%, but only before any coin is tossed. Once four heads have landed, they are no longer unknown, so their probability is now 1. Whatever the run so far, the chance it continues for one more toss is always 0.5. Expecting the fifth toss to lean toward tails because of the four heads before it is exactly the fallacy.

paragraphs.heading: Every sequence is equally likely
paragraphs.text: Flip a fair coin 21 times. Twenty heads followed by one tail is no more likely than 21 heads: each comes up with probability 1 in 2,097,152, which is 0.5²¹. Every other 21-flip sequence has that same chance. So there is no reason to think earlier flips shift the odds of later ones.

paragraphs.heading: Monte Carlo, 1913
paragraphs.text: The fallacy's other name comes from the Monte Carlo Casino, where on August 18, 1913, a roulette ball landed on black 26 times in a row. On a single-zero wheel, a run of 26 reds or 26 blacks has a chance of about 1 in 68.4 million, if the wheel is unbiased. Gamblers lost millions of francs betting against black. They wrongly believed the streak had thrown the wheel's randomness off balance, so a long run of red had to follow.

paragraphs.heading: When the past does matter
paragraphs.text: The fallacy concerns independent events only. When events depend on each other, past results can change future chances. Draw an ace from a deck and keep it out, and the next card is less likely to be an ace: if the ace was the first card drawn, the chance of another ace is now 3/51 (5.88%), down from 4/52 (7.69%), while every other rank climbs to 4/51 (7.84%). This effect is what lets card counting work in blackjack. And a gambler who sees tails again and again may sensibly decide the coin might not be fair; that is sound Bayesian reasoning, not the fallacy.

paragraphs.heading: Looking backwards
paragraphs.text: Ian Hacking described an inverse version: someone walks into a room, sees a double six rolled, and wrongly decides the dice must have been rolling for a long time. A related retrospective version reasons about an unseen past result, such as deciding that an earlier hidden flip was tails after seeing several heads. Three studies of Stanford University students found that people do show the fallacy about the past as well as the future.

paragraphs.heading: An old mistake
paragraphs.text: In 1796 Pierre-Simon Laplace wrote about men eager for a son who grew anxious hearing of boys born in the month they expected to become fathers. They thought boys and girls should even out by the end of each month, so the boys already born made a girl more likely for them. This essay is seen as one of the earliest descriptions of the fallacy. In the same way, some parents with several children of one sex wrongly believe a child of the other sex is due.
